$comment: Real, precomputed HMAC-SHA256 vectors per spec/05-webhooks.md and Invariant I11 (spec/02-invariants.md#i11). raw_body is the exact byte sequence the signature was computed over: a runtime must compute against this exact string, not a re-serialized/re-parsed form of it. Every runtime must reproduce signature_hex and signature_base64 exactly from raw_body and secret, and must reject the tampered-body and missing-header cases below using a constant-time comparison.

tampered_body.description: Body was altered after signing (amount changed from 100.00 to 999.00); the signature header still carries the signature computed over the original raw_body above.
tampered_body.why: Recomputing HMAC-SHA256 over received_body with the same secret yields 1efabea4b8371fa359a0b67de24077f78d571d739003eecbb7360e9cc430a7e8, which does not match the received signature.

missing_header.description: The signature header is absent entirely from the inbound request.
missing_header.why: A missing signature header is a rejection, never an implicit pass-through. See spec/05-webhooks.md.

reordered_but_logically_equal_body.description: A body with the same fields in a different order and different whitespace, illustrating why verification must run against the exact raw bytes rather than a re-serialized form.
reordered_but_logically_equal_body.why: The signature was computed over raw_body's exact bytes. Even though this body is logically equivalent field-for-field, its bytes differ (key order and whitespace), so recomputing HMAC-SHA256 over it does not reproduce the received signature. A runtime that reformats the body before verifying would wrongly reject a legitimate differently-formatted request in one direction, and wrongly accept a forged one in the other, which is exactly why verification must run over the untouched raw body.

wrong_algorithm.description: The inbound signature was actually computed with HMAC-SHA1 against the same secret and raw_body, not HMAC-SHA256, e.g. because the sender's own signing code has a bug or is misconfigured relative to what this manifest declares.
wrong_algorithm.why: Recomputing HMAC-SHA256 (per the manifest's declared scheme) over raw_body yields 1dbf340e95462dcd89205a804462455b50c7e1db394b7f1bdf08316c9175af71, a completely different value (and a different length: SHA-1 produces 20 bytes/40 hex characters, SHA-256 produces 32 bytes/64 hex characters) from the received HMAC-SHA1 signature. A runtime must reject this the same way it rejects any other mismatch, not attempt to detect and fall back to a different algorithm: the scheme a manifest declares is the only one ever computed against.

malformed_signature_encoding.description: The signature header is present but its value is not valid hex at all (contains a non-hex character) for a scheme requiring hex.
malformed_signature_encoding.why: A signature value that cannot even be decoded per the declared scheme's encoding must be rejected the same way an incorrect-but-well-formed signature is: a decoding failure is not a distinct third outcome, and must never be treated as an error that bypasses verification (e.g. by skipping the comparison and accepting the request).

malformed_signature_encoding_base64.description: The signature header is present but its value is not valid base64 at all, for a scheme requiring base64.
malformed_signature_encoding_base64.why: Same reasoning as the hex case above, for the base64 scheme.

scheme_none_always_verifies.description: webhook.verification.scheme: none (only meaningful for a provider with no signing mechanism at all, e.g. providers/mock) always treats the inbound body as verified, regardless of whether any signature-shaped header is present.
scheme_none_always_verifies.why: There is no secret and no signature_header to check for scheme: none (schema/manifest.v1.schema.json does not require either field in this case); this is a real gap for a provider with an actual signing mechanism the manifest simply hasn't captured, and spec/05-webhooks.md calls it out as a red flag on any non-mock provider, not a mechanism to lean on for a provider that does sign its callbacks.
